title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Reference Architectures, Packaging, and Day‑2 Operations
author: Claire Zhang
body:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended reference architectures, packaging patterns, and day‑2 operational procedures for Private Deployments (VPC and on‑prem). It covers network requirements, reference architectures by deployment size, on‑prem packaging and air‑gapped install guidance, operational runbooks for monitoring and backups, and step‑by‑step upgrade and rollback procedures. Intended audience: infra engineers, platform engineers, and customer‑facing solutions engineers.

Scope

- Applies to all Private Deployment engagements (VPC, private cloud, and on‑prem appliance).
- Excludes hosted API and Dedicated multi‑tenant environments.
- Covers deployment patterns, configuration examples, operational checklists, and safe upgrade/rollback procedures.

Goals

- Provide repeatable, secure reference architectures that meet common enterprise requirements.
- Minimize downtime and data risk during upgrades via validated procedures and fallbacks.
- Standardize packaging and installation steps so Solutions and Support teams can operate consistently.

Reference architectures

1) Small / Edge deployment (POC, < 10 concurrent requests)

- Architecture: single control plane node + 1 GPU serving node (NVIDIA T4/A10) in customer VPC or on‑prem rack. Optional NFS for model artifacts.
- Network: single private subnet, NAT for outbound updates (or offline bundle).
- Recommended Sizing: 1x m6.large equivalent control, 1x GPU with 16‑32 GB VRAM.
- Availability: single AZ, best effort.

2) Medium deployment (production, 10‑200 qps)

- Architecture: HA control plane (3 control nodes), 2‑4 GPU serving nodes, autoscaling pool for stateless workers, ingress (ALB) with WAF.
- Network: separate subnets for control, serving, and management. Private endpoint for customer services.
- Storage: replicated object store (S3 compatible) or clustered PV for artifacts and model caching.
- Availability: multi‑AZ recommended for resiliency.

3) Large / Enterprise (multi‑region, >200 qps, regulatory needs)

- Architecture: multi‑region control plane (active/passive or active/active globals), dedicated GPU pools per region, intelligent routing by latency/cost, disaster recovery site with cross‑region replication.
- Security: dedicated KMS/HSM for keys, private connectivity (Direct Connect/ExpressRoute), strict RBAC and network segmentation.
- Compliance: audit logging to customer SIEM, retention policy attachments.

Network and security prerequisites

- IP addressing: allocate non‑overlapping CIDRs for control, serving, and management subnets.
- Firewall rules: allow the following minimum egress/ingress (example):
  - Control plane -> NTP (UDP 123), DNS (53), object store (443)
  - Ingress load balancer -> serving nodes: TCP 443 (TLS)
  - Prometheus/Grafana scraping: control‑plane -> metrics (TCP 9090/9100) over management network only
- Ports and services table:

  | Service | Direction | Protocol | Port(s) | Notes |
  |--------|-----------|----------|---------|-------|
  | Ingress TLS | Inbound | TCP | 443 | ALB/NLB to serving |
  | Healthchecks | Inbound | TCP | 8080 | Internal health endpoints |
  | Model artifact sync | Outbound | HTTPS | 443 | S3/Minio endpoints |
  | Inter-node RPC | Bi‑dir | TCP | 50051 | gRPC internal API |

- Identity & secrets:
  - Integrate with customer KMS where required; store keys in HSM/KMS and do not persist plaintext secrets.
  - Use short‑lived service credentials and mTLS between internal components.

On‑prem packaging and air‑gapped installation

Packaging formats supported

- Docker images (OCI compliant): recommended for most environments. We provide prebuilt images with signed manifests.
- Tarball bundles: for air‑gapped installs, bundles include container images (OCI layout), Helm charts, and offline artifacts index.
- OS packages (RPM/DEB): available for customers who manage at the OS level (for control plane components only).

Air‑gapped install checklist

1) Customer provides an isolated artifact transfer mechanism (USB, internal registry, or secure import node).
2) Redwood provides an offline bundle: images.tar (OCI layout), helm‑charts.tgz, artifacts‑index.json, checksums, and PGP signature.
3) Customer verifies signatures and uploads images into local registry:

   $ skopeo copy --all docker-archive:images.tar docker://local.registry.internal/redwood

4) Install control plane from local charts:

   $ helm install redwood-control ./helm/redwood-control --set image.registry=local.registry.internal

5) Validate integrity with signatures and run acceptance tests (see Appendix).

Package signing and verification

- All release bundles are signed with Redwood release key. Customers should verify with the published public key. Example:

   $ gpg --verify redwood-release-20270623.tar.gz.sig redwood-release-20270623.tar.gz

Day‑2 operations (monitoring, backups, scaling, and maintenance)

Monitoring and observability

- Metrics: token latency P50/P95/P99, per‑model throughput, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, queue length.
- Logging: structured JSON logs to stdout, forwarded to customer SIEM.
- Dashboards: prebuilt Grafana dashboards for per‑route latency, per‑GPU metrics, and cost breakdown.
- Alerts & SLOs:
  - Request latency P95 target: < 300ms for short requests (<= 512 tokens)
  - Error rate SLO: < 0.5% per service per 24h
  - GPU memory pressure alert: > 85% sustained for 5m

Backups and artifact retention

- Model artifacts: store primary copy in object store; periodic snapshots to secondary location.
- Control plane metadata: Postgres backups (logical + base backups) daily with WAL archiving.
- Retention policy: default 30 days for metadata, 365 days for audit logs (configurable).

Scaling policies

- Serving nodes should scale based on per‑GPU queue length and avg per‑token throughput. Recommended autoscaler triggers:
  - Add node if avg queue length > 50 for 30s
  - Remove node if avg queue length < 10 for 5 minutes and GPU utilization < 30%

Maintenance windows and patching

- Regular maintenance windows: weekly low‑traffic window agreed with customer.
- Kernel/OS patching: use blue/green or rolling updates with drain scheduling for serving nodes.

Upgrade procedure (control plane and serving runtime)

Principles

- All upgrades must be tested in a staging environment that mirrors customer config.
- Apply upgrades in phases: control plane (canary), serving runtime (canary pools), global rollout.

High‑level steps

1) Pre‑upgrade validation (run acceptance tests and snapshot DB):
   - Snapshot Postgres: pg_dump and base backup.
   - Export current helm values: helm get values redwood-control -o yaml > values-$(date +%F).yaml
2) Canary control plane upgrade (single control node):
   - Scale control plane to 3 nodes if not already.
   - Upgrade one node and validate control plane health and API compatibility for 30‑60 minutes.
3) Upgrade serving canary pool (1 node or 5% of capacity):
   - Deploy new runtime image to canary pool.
   - Run synthetic traffic and compare latency and output quality (auto regression tests).
4) Gradual rollout: increase to 25% -> 50% -> 100% with validation gates at each step.

Example helm upgrade command

$ helm upgrade redwood-control ./helm/redwood-control --namespace redwood --values values-20270315.yaml --set image.tag=2027.03.15

Validation gates

- Liveness and readiness probes must pass for 15 consecutive checks.
- No increase in 5xx errors by > 0.2% vs baseline.
- Latency P95 for canary <= baseline P95 + 10%
- Model output quality regression: run prompt set A; monitor BLEU/ROUGE/semantic similarity thresholds.

Rollback procedure (control plane and serving runtime)

When to rollback

- Critical functional regression (failing acceptance tests)
- Service error rate spike > 1% sustained for 15 minutes
- Latency degradation beyond acceptable SLOs impacting customer SLA

Rollback steps (serving runtime)

1) Pause rollout and mark new image as suspect.
2) Redirect traffic back to previous stable fleet (via routing policy).
3) Re-deploy previous image tag to canary and validate.
4) If control plane change required rollback, restore DB from pre‑upgrade backup and restart control plane with previous helm values.

Example rollback commands

# Revert to previous image tag for serving pool
$ kubectl set image deployment/redwood-serving redwood-serving=local.registry.internal/redwood-serving:2027.02.01 -n redwood

# Restore Postgres logical backup (example)
$ pg_restore -d redwood_prod --clean --no-owner preupgrade-2027-03-15.dump

Customer requirements library (checklist)

Below is a checklist to use during sales and pre‑sales to capture minimum customer commitments and environment readiness.

- Network & Connectivity
  - Non‑overlapping CIDRs allocated for control, serving, management (Y/N)
  - Customer provides NAT/egress or accepts offline bundle (Y/N)
  - Ports opened per requirements table (Y/N)
- Identity & Secrets
  - KMS/HSM integration available (Y/N)
  - RBAC and SSO provider details (Okta, Azure AD, etc.)
- Storage & Backups
  - Object store endpoint and credentials provided (Y/N)
  - Backup retention policy defined (days)
- Compliance & Audit
  - SIEM integration available (Y/N)
  - Data residency requirements (region/country)
- Operational Support
  - Maintenance window agreed (day/time)
  - Onsite staff or remote access for troubleshooting (Y/N)

Ownership and runbooks

- Primary owner: Redwood Solutions Engineering for initial deployment and handoff.
- Day‑2 owner: customer platform team for routine ops; Redwood SRE for critical escalations per contract.
- Runbooks (links):
  - Incident runbook: confluence://eng-sre/incident-process (internal)
  - Backup & restore: confluence://eng-private-deployments/private-deployments-day2-upgrade-rollback-2026.json
  - Upgrade checklist: confluence://eng-private-deployments/private-deployments-deployment-day2-ops-upgrade-rollback-2027-08-01.json

Appendix: example YAML snippets and commands

- Model cache config (example helm values snippet):

  modelCache:
    type: s3
    endpoint: https://minio.internal
    bucket: redwood-models
    region: us‑west-2

- Example healthcheck curl (control plane):

  $ curl -sSf -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://redwood-control.internal/api/v1/healthz

Acceptance tests (minimum)

- Smoke test: control API returns 200 for /healthz and /version
- Latency smoke: sample prompt < 512 tokens returns in < 1s (small deployment target)
- Functional test: run canonical prompt set and verify outputs are within acceptance thresholds

FAQ and troubleshooting notes

- Q: Can we run without outbound internet?
  - A: Yes. Use the offline bundle and local registry; ensure local time sync and DNS resolution for internal services.
- Q: What if a runtime change causes model quality regression?
  - A: Immediately halt rollout, route traffic to previous model, and create a regression triage ticket with the Applied ML and Evals team.
